title: Equipment Pre-Use Checks
summary: OSHA requires frequent and regular inspections of job sites, materials and equipment. This talk covers what employers must do and what crews should do when equipment does not pass.
talking_points: Employers must set up programs for frequent and regular inspections of job sites, materials and equipment.
Competent persons designated by the employer make those inspections.
Good practice, not a stated requirement of 1926.20: check your tool or machine before each use so problems are found before work starts.
Machinery, tools, material or equipment that does not comply with OSHA construction requirements may not be used.
Noncompliant equipment must be tagged as unsafe, have its controls locked to make it inoperable, or be physically removed from where it operates.
Only employees qualified by training or experience may operate equipment and machinery.
Under 1926.20(a)(1), contractors may not require a laborer or mechanic to work in surroundings or conditions that are unsanitary, hazardous, or dangerous to health or safety.
If a piece of equipment fails the check, tell your supervisor. Do not use it.
site_hazards_to_check: Equipment with no recent inspection by a competent person
Tools or machines with missing guards, damaged parts or failed safety devices
Damaged equipment that is not tagged, locked out or removed
Operators without the training or experience for the equipment
Unsafe equipment mixed in with good equipment in the same area
discussion_questions: Who is the designated competent person for equipment inspections on this job?
What do we check on our equipment before we use it each day?
How do we tag or lock out a machine that fails a check?

attribution.notice: Adapted from 29 CFR 1926.20, General safety and health provisions. Reproduced with attribution for jobsite safety training; not an endorsement by OSHA.

flags: Points 1, 2, 4, 5, 6 quote-accurate to 1926.20(b)(2)-(4). Concern checked: 1926.20 requires frequent and regular inspections by competent persons, not inspection before each use.

FIXES MADE: (1) point 3 now labels pre-use checks as good practice rather than an OSHA requirement (the summary already said frequent and regular inspections). (2) Point 7 was a bare absolute quoting 1926.20(a)(1), a Section 107 contract condition; reworded to attribute it to the paragraph. Added 1926.20(a)(1) to osha_standards.

Non-blocking: content is mostly a paraphrase of the regulation with few concrete pre-use check items (cord, guard, controls, fluid, tags); consider adding a short generic checklist. Public domain, osha.gov. No UK wording.
